A1.justification: Both PDFs describe MindLLM and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures and appendices. The retained material can be matched across versions, including Appendices A-D in v1 and A-I in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original captioning, question-answering, held-out-subject generalization, task-adaptation and ablation results, plus qualitative examples in Appendix D.

after.justification: v2 retains original experiments and adds subject-count scaling, runtime measurements, downstream ablations, additional-subject results and representation visualizations.

M1.justification: Sections 3.1-3.3 retain the same learned-query attention, positional and parcellation keys, voxel-signal values, MLP, frozen Vicuna-7b and BIT training objective. The architecture hyperparameters also match; the new comparisons and analyses do not establish an algorithm change.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same eight-subject NSD population, 15-source BIT collection and downstream tasks, including TDIUC. The added subject-count experiments and subject-specific results use existing coverage rather than introducing another dataset, population or task.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds the subject-agnostic UniBrain of Wang et al. (2024b), alongside the retained, distinct UniBrain of Mai and Zhang (2023). Tables 2-4 retain their comparator sets. Table 10 additionally compares runtime among already-used encoders.

E3.justification: v2 adds training-subject sweeps of 1, 3, 5 and 7 with evaluation on seen Subject 1 and held-out Subject 8 (Tables 5-6). It also introduces downstream ablation evaluation without task-specific fine-tuning, including perplexity (Table 11), and separate encoder/LLM timing procedures (Table 10). Existing benchmark protocols are largely retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends the retained validation-loss ablation and qualitative examples. New analyses test sensitivity to training-subject count, downstream consequences of key-embedding choices, computational overhead, layer-by-layer subject clustering through t-SNE, and attention-pattern consistency across subjects (Tables 5-6, 10-11; Figures 10-11).

E5.justification: Both versions retain the same random-seed stability statement and maximum ±0.3 variation for paragraph-captioning BLEU-1. v2 adds no run counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or systematic uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Table 3 revises 36 of 38 MindLLM scores under the same reported split while retaining baseline scores: ST-VQA ANLS changes from 10.97 to 13.63, and COCO-caption BLEU-1/CIDEr from 47.30/6.41 to 44.60/13.22. Table 2 revises paragraph-caption METEOR/CIDEr entries for from-scratch MindLLM and BIT-trained MindBridge. Substantial new results cover scaling, runtime, downstream ablations and Subjects 2, 5 and 7.

T1.justification: The method equations and MindLLM complexity derivation remain unchanged. Appendix C/Table 10 adds explicit asymptotic complexity expressions for UMBRAE, MindBridge and UniBrain, extending the mathematical comparison without adding a theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction strengthen the reported unseen-subject improvement from 16.4% to 24.5%. The central contributions of subject-agnostic encoding and versatile BIT decoding, and the 12.0% downstream and 25.0% adaptation claims, remain unchanged.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations linking progressive MLP representation mixing to generalization and cross-subject attention similarity to shared brain organization. It explains runtime overhead relative to the shared LLM and suggests domain adaptation as future work. The existing static-fMRI limitation and principal neuroscientific interpretations remain.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability URL, discloses eight days of instruction tuning on the previously specified eight L40S GPUs, and identifies Table 2 as Subject 1 results. Table 10 provides approximate model sizes for runtime analysis. Existing architecture hyperparameters move from v1 Table 8 into prose without changing.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds a paragraph positioning MindLLM against image, video, speech and music decoding and reverse-direction work. New citations support structural-functional correspondence and prospective domain adaptation. Appendix F adds an architecture-property comparison, while the central positioning against existing fMRI encoders remains intact.

P1.justification: Most existing prose and the main narrative are retained. v2 makes local grammar corrections, adds a scaling subsection and Appendices E-I, expands Appendix C, and adds acknowledgments and an impact statement. Hyperparameter information is converted from a table into prose.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the displays with scaling, runtime, ablation, architecture-comparison and additional-subject tables, plus two new visualization figures. The original attention maps are redesigned from a horizontal blue panel into a red two-row display with hemisphere and orientation annotations. The unchanged loss curve is renumbered, qualitative figures are relocated, and the hyperparameter table becomes prose.

improvement.justification: Downstream ablations, additional-subject results and code/training disclosures improve validation and reproducibility beyond v1. However, v2 leaves an unexplained discrepancy between Tables 3 and 6 for seven-subject training with held-out Subject 8: captioning CIDEr is 13.22 versus 6.41. This limits confidence in the strengthened generalization headline and tempers the benefits of the added evidence.
